name: Rastafari
info: Rastafari is an Abrahamic religion that developed among Afro-Jamaicans in the 1930s, centred on belief in one God, Jah, and on Haile Selassie, Emperor of Ethiopia, and known for its Afrocentric outlook, its livity and its music.

facts.origin: Jamaica, in the 1930s, among impoverished and socially disenfranchised Afro-Jamaican communities, after clergymen proclaimed that Haile Selassie's 1930 crowning as Emperor of Ethiopia fulfilled biblical prophecy.
facts.founder: none: there is no single founder and no leader followed by all Rastafari. Early preachers who proclaimed Haile Selassie the returned Jesus included Leonard Howell, Archibald Dunkley, Robert Hinds and Joseph Hibbert, and Howell was the early movement's leading figure.
facts.scriptures: The Bible, often read literally and as cryptographic, with the Book of Revelation seen as especially important; also Leonard Howell's The Promised Key (1935), Robert Athlyi Rogers' Holy Piby (1924), Fitz Balintine Pettersburg's Royal Parchment Scroll of Black Supremacy (1920s) and, for many Rastas, the 14th-century Ethiopian Kebra Nagast.
facts.followers: An estimated 700,000 to 1,000,000 worldwide in 2012; 29,026 people identified as Rastas in Jamaica's 2011 census, and about 5,000 in England and Wales in the 2001 census.

t: Rastas worship one God, Jah, whom they hold to be present within each individual; they accord key importance to Haile Selassie, whom many see as the Second Coming of Jesus and Jah incarnate and others as a human prophet.

Rastafari is Afrocentric: it teaches that the African diaspora lives in exile in "Babylon", meaning Western society, and many Rastas look to Africa as "Zion", although since the 1980s many understand the return in a metaphorical sense.

There is no central authority, no creed and no professional priesthood. Rastas call their practices "livity", and the movement is divided into "mansions", of which the Nyabinghi, the Bobo Ashanti and the Twelve Tribes of Israel are the most prominent.
dyk: Many Rastas speak of "knowing" Jah rather than "believing" in him, and they use "I" in place of "me", "I and I" in place of "we" and "downpression" in place of "oppression", because oppression bears down on people rather than lifting them up.
ev: Haile Selassie is crowned Emperor of Ethiopia, and several Jamaican clergymen claim that it fulfils biblical prophecy and shows that he is a black messiah
Jamaica's colonial authorities arrest Leonard Howell and charge him with sedition, and he is imprisoned for two years
Howell forms a Rasta community known as Pinnacle in Saint Catherine Parish, which the police raid repeatedly and which closes in 1954
After the first Rastafarian Universal Convention in Back-o-Wall, Kingston, Rasta militants unsuccessfully try to capture the city in Haile Selassie's name
Haile Selassie visits Jamaica at its government's invitation, and thousands of Rastas gather to see his arrival at the airport
Haile Selassie dies a year after his overthrow by the Derg, which causes a crisis of faith for many practitioners
The first international assembly of Rastafari groups takes place in Toronto, Canada
Jamaica decriminalises personal possession of marijuana up to two ounces

sections.origins:
Rastafari is an Abrahamic religion that developed among impoverished and socially disenfranchised Afro-Jamaican communities in Jamaica during the 1930s, in reaction to the colonial culture that then dominated the island. It grew out of the legacy of the Atlantic slave trade; slavery was abolished in the Caribbean island in 1834, although racial prejudice remained prevalent. Scholars have called it a new religious movement, a social movement, an Afro-Caribbean religion and a Creole religion rooted in African, European and Indian practices, while many Rastas prefer to call it a "way of life", a "philosophy" or a "spirituality". Its name comes from "Ras Tafari Makonnen", the pre-regnal title of Haile Selassie, and it is unknown why the early Rastas chose this form of his name.

Christian Revivalism, including the Great Revival of 1860–61, Ethiopianism and the Back to Africa ethos, both with 18th-century roots, and the activism of Marcus Garvey all contributed. After Haile Selassie was crowned Emperor of Ethiopia in 1930, several Jamaican clergymen claimed that this was evidence that he was a black messiah prophesied in the Book of Revelation, the Book of Daniel and Psalms. Street preachers, among them Leonard Howell, Archibald Dunkley, Robert Hinds and Joseph Hibbert, began to say that he was the returned Jesus, first in Kingston and then across Jamaica, especially among poor communities hit by the Great Depression. Peter B. Clarke stated that "to all intents and purposes this was the beginning" of Rastafari. Garvey, whom Rastas hold in great esteem and often regard as a prophet, knew of the religion but took a largely negative view of it.
sections.beliefs:
Rastas call their worldview "Rastalogy", but no summary of it has been given the status of a catechism or creed, and no Rasta has the authority to declare which beliefs are orthodox. Rastas are monotheists who worship a single God, Jah, a shortened form of "Jehovah". They believe in his immanence, summed up in the aphorism "God is man and man is God". They regard Jesus as a black African and reject the common depiction of him as a white European. Rastas accord key importance to Haile Selassie, Emperor of Ethiopia from 1930 to 1974. Many see him as the Second Coming of Jesus and Jah incarnate, while others regard him as a messenger of God or a human prophet. Members of the Twelve Tribes of Israel hold that the Second Coming has yet to occur. In a 1967 interview Selassie, who described himself as a devout Christian, said that he was a man and mortal.

Rastafari is Afrocentric. Rastas identify with the ancient Israelites and, for most of them, black Africans are God's chosen people. They teach that the African diaspora lives in exile in "Babylon", their term for Western society, and they see Zion as an ideal, applied to Ethiopia, to Africa more broadly, to Jamaica or to a state of mind. For its first three decades the religion stressed return to Africa; by its fourth decade many Rastas understood this metaphorically, and the phrase "liberation before repatriation" came into use. Rastafari is also millenarian: many Rastas expect Babylon to be overthrown on a Day of Judgment and a new age of peace and justice to follow. Views on race vary, and black supremacy, common early in the movement, has waned since at least the 1970s.
sections.texts:
Like Christianity, Rastafari treats the Bible as a holy book central to its belief system. Rastas often read it literally and use it as a source book from which to form their own beliefs and practices. They commonly believe that the Bible was originally written on stone in the Ethiopian language of Amharic, a belief that runs contrary to scholarly understandings of the Bible's history. They hold that its true meaning has been warped by mistranslation and by deliberate manipulation by those seeking to deny black Africans their history, and they regard it as cryptographic, with hidden meanings that intuition and meditation on the "book within" can reveal. The Book of Revelation is often seen as particularly important for understanding the world's present situation.

Because of what they regard as the Bible's corruption, Rastas also turn to other sources that they believe shed light on African history. These include Leonard Howell's 1935 work The Promised Key, Robert Athlyi Rogers' 1924 book Holy Piby and Fitz Balintine Pettersburg's 1920s work, the Royal Parchment Scroll of Black Supremacy. Many Rastas also treat the Kebra Nagast, a 14th-century Ethiopian text, as a source through which to interpret the Bible.

Music is the movement's chief means of communication. Rasta songs are sung to praise and commune with Jah, and many use the tunes of older Christian hymns. Rastas also have their own language, called "dread talk", "Iyaric" or "Rasta talk", developed in Jamaica in the 1940s.
sections.spread:
During the 1950s Rastafari grew rapidly in Jamaica and spread to other Caribbean islands, the United States and Britain. In the 1960s and 1970s it gained respectability in Jamaica and visibility abroad through the popularity of Rastafari-inspired reggae musicians, most notably Bob Marley. In the mid-1970s Prime Minister Michael Manley used Rasta imagery to bolster his popularity, and Rasta symbols became increasingly mainstream in Jamaican society. Enthusiasm declined in the 1980s after the deaths of Selassie in 1975 and Marley in 1981, when Pentecostal and other Charismatic Christian groups attracted more young recruits in Jamaica. The movement has survived and has a presence in many parts of the world.

Jamaican migrants took Rastafari to the United States and Canada in the 1960s and 1970s. It spread across the eastern Caribbean in the 1970s, and Rastas took part in Grenada's New Jewel Movement of 1979. Small communities exist in Brazil, Panama and Nicaragua. Caribbean Rastas first arrived in Ghana in the 1960s, and a Rasta settlement was established in Shashamane, Ethiopia, on land made available through Haile Selassie's Ethiopian World Federation; it peaked at 2,000 people and declined to around 200. There were at least 12,000 Rastas in South Africa in 2008. In the United Kingdom, Rastafari attracted converts among the second generation of British Caribbean people by the late 1960s. It has also appeared in continental Europe, New Zealand, Australia, Japan and Israel. It has spread mainly in Anglophone regions, largely because reggae is produced in English.
sections.community:
Rastafari has no single administrative structure and no single leader, and most Rastas avoid centralised, hierarchical structures because they do not want to replicate those of Babylon. It has no professional priesthood, since Rastas believe that no mediator is needed between the worshipper and Jah, but it does have "elders", an honorific for Rastas of good reputation. Rastas hold "groundings", meetings with drumming, chanting, hymns, reasoning and, often, the smoking of cannabis, which is regarded as a sacrament. The largest gatherings, called Nyabinghi Issemblies, usually last between three and seven days. Rastas follow "ital" dietary rules, many wear dreadlocks and most avoid alcohol and hard drugs. The movement has traditionally presented women as subordinate to men, a pattern that has changed since the 1970s with a growing "womanist" movement.

Its subdivisions are called "houses" or "mansions". The House of Nyabinghi, probably the largest, keeps closest to the movement's 1940s form. The Bobo Ashanti was founded by Emanuel Charles Edwards in 1958, and the Twelve Tribes of Israel by Vernon Carrington in 1968; it is regarded as the most liberal form and closest to Christianity.

For its first thirty years Rastafari was in conflict with Jamaica's authorities. Police often arrested Rastas for cannabis possession, and in 1958 militants tried to capture Kingston and Spanish Town. The Coral Gardens incident of 1963 led to several deaths, and in 1964 the government introduced tougher cannabis laws. In 1989 a British Industrial Tribunal concluded that Rastafarians could be considered an ethnic group under the Race Relations Act 1976.
sections.legacy:
Rastafari's social influence has been more substantial than its numbers, particularly in fostering a racial, political and cultural consciousness among the African diaspora and Africans themselves. Internationally it has been most popular among the poor and marginalised youth, and by valorising Africa and blackness it offers young people in the diaspora a positive identity. Its music shaped ska, reggae and dub. Reggae drew on Rasta rhythms, chants, language and social critiques and gained wide international popularity in the mid-1970s; many Rastas grew critical of it, believing it had commercialised their religion, and most Rastas do not listen to reggae. Rasta terms have also entered wider Jamaican speech.

In Jamaica, Rastas are no longer only the poor: after 1965 the religion attracted many middle-class members, and by the 1980s some Rastas worked as lawyers and university professors. In the 1980s Barbara Makeda Blake Hannah became a Rasta senator in Jamaica's Parliament. From the 1990s Jamaican Rastas organised politically, and in 1995 the Rastafari Centralization Organization was established. Rastas have campaigned for the legalisation of cannabis: Jamaica decriminalised personal possession of up to two ounces in 2015, and Barbados legalised its use in religious settings in 2019.

Rastas have also won legal battles over the right to wear dreadlocks, among them a 2020 ruling by the High Court of Malawi that all public schools must allow them. Rastafari is legally recognised as a religion in various countries, and many Rastas travel to Jamaica as a pilgrimage to the fountain-head of their faith.

summary: Rastafari is an Abrahamic religion that arose among Afro-Jamaicans in the 1930s after clergymen proclaimed Haile Selassie's crowning as Emperor of Ethiopia a fulfilment of prophecy. Rastas worship Jah, see Africa as Zion and the West as Babylon, and have no central authority. Reggae carried its themes worldwide, and an estimated 700,000 to 1 million Rastas live today.
references: Leonard E. Barrett, The Rastafarians (Beacon Press, 1997)
Barry Chevannes, Rastafari: Roots and Ideology (Syracuse University Press, 1994)
Ennis B. Edmonds, Rastafari: A Very Short Introduction (Oxford University Press, 2012)
Ennis B. Edmonds, Rastafari: From Outcasts to Cultural Bearers (Oxford University Press, 2008)
Hélène Lee, First Rasta: Leonard Howell and the Rise of Rastafarianism (Chicago Review Press, 2004)
notes: Source: the Rastafari article only; its Further reading and Sources lists are empty in the saved text, so references are left empty for the editor.
Start 1930 (circa): the article says the religion developed during the 1930s and dates the preachers' proclamations to the years after Selassie's 1930 crowning; Clarke calls this the beginning.

Event 1966: the article gives April 1966 for Selassie's visit; 1958 is the year of the first Rastafarian Universal Convention and of the attempts on Kingston and Spanish Town. The 1982 Toronto assembly is the article's first international assembly.
The article gives the Pinnacle community's closing as 1954, when Howell was committed to a mental hospital; this is mentioned in an event only, not detailed.
Selassie's body: the article says it was buried beneath his palace and found in 1992, and that some Rastas denied his death; this was left out for length.

Not detailed: the 1957 killing allegation, gender and sexuality teachings, and the Bobo Ashanti's former teachings of black superiority; the article gives them but they were left for length. The article describes the Nyabinghi gatherings and ganja use only in general terms, as followed here.
A 'Hispanic studies scholars' classification as a Creole religion is attributed to no named scholars in the text for brevity; it is Fernández Olmos and Paravisini-Gebert's phrase.

Faith map: coordinates are mine for places the article names. Years of areas are the article's where it gives them (1930s Jamaica, 1950s Caribbean, Britain and the US, 1960s North America and Ghana and Shashamane, 1970s eastern Caribbean, 2008 South Africa); the 1950 start for Britain and the US, 1964 for Ghana and 1975 for the eastern Caribbean are the nearest dates the article supports.
